newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU blesses BT Swiss deal, to act soon on MCI.
newsitem.headline: EU blesses BT Swiss deal, to act soon on MCI.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc on Thursday continued its successful march towards building up a global network as the European Commission cleared its Swiss telecoms venture with Tele Danmark A/S and three Swiss firms.
The EU's competition watchdog is also expected to clear BT's $20 billion merger with MCI Communications Corp of the United States next month albeit with minor changes.

The Swiss venture called Newtelco -- involving Swiss national railway company SBB, supermarket chain Migros and Union Bank of Switzerland -- operates the second national telecommunications system in Switzerland.

The Commission said in statement that the venture would have no "significant effect" on competition in Europe. Tele Danmark has a 29 percent stake and BT a 20 percent stake in the group, which was launched last year.

The British telecoms giant wants to form a vast network of alliances to take advantage of the full liberalisation of the sector in Europe in January 1998 and to adapt to the globalisation of the market.

Its alliance plans have met with little EU regulatory opposition, unlike similar moves by the French and German telecoms operators to unite against nascent competition, because the British market is one of the most liberalised in Europe.

The remedies sought in the merger with MCI are to centre on audio and teleconferencing in Britain, where BT has a dominant position, and access to the partners' transatlantic cable capacity, Commission sources have said.

The merger will give BT control of MCI, in which it already has a 20-percent stake, to create the world's second largest telecoms group based on market capitalisation behind Japan's NTT Corp and neck-and-neck with U.S. long-distance calls leader AT&T.
Under the terms of the deal announced in November the two companies will be merged in their existing Concert joint venture. The plan received the formal blessing of BT shareholders earlier this week.

It must still receive the green light in the United States where legislation forbids a foreign company from taking more than 20 percent in a U.S. company unless its home market is effectively open to competition.
AT&T has argued with antitrust authorities on both sides of the Atlantic that there are still barriers to entry the British market citing in particular BT's easier access to international traffic.

BT further expanded its global alliance network earlier this week when it announced a deal with Portugal Telecom SA. This is expected to be followed by a similar agreement with neighbouring country's Telefonica de Espana giving it a foothold in Latin America with which both Portugal and Spain maintain privileged links.
